newsitem.title: USA: Palm Beach Cty, Fla., would be 6th biggest default.
newsitem.headline: Palm Beach Cty, Fla., would be 6th biggest default.

text.p: If a power plant partnership defaults on $288.5 million of Palm Beach County industrial development bonds, it would be the biggest municipal bond default in Florida and one of the 10 largest in the nation, according to the Bond Investors Association.
"We figure it's about No. 6 (nationally)," BIA President Richard Lehman told Reuters Monday. "There's not question this is the largest in Florida."
The bonds are already in technical default because the partnership that owns the power plants filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on May 14.

No payments have been missed. Officials handling the bonds for SunTrust Bank Inc, the bond trustee, could not be reached for comment on whether the next debt service payment would be made on schedule on June 1.

"If they do, they would be making it out of escrow funds, out of the money the bondholders originally paid in to begin with," said Lehman, whose group tracks bond defaults. "They're not having any revenues coming in. That's why they filed Chapter 11."
The bonds in question are three series of Palm Beach County Industrial Development Revenue bonds:
--Okeelanta Power Limited Partnership Project, Series 1993A, prinicpal of $160 million.
--Osceola Power Limited Partnership Project, tax-exempt series 1994A, principal of $120.5 million.
--Osceola Power Limited Partnership Project, taxable Series 1994 B, principal amount of $8 million.
No county funds were pledged to the bonds, which financed construction of two cogeneration plants owned by the Okeelanta Power and Gator Generating Company Limited Partnerships.
The partnerships are affiliated with Pacific Gas & Electric Co, a unit of PG&E Corp and Bechtel Enterprises and Flo-Sun Inc, one of Florida's largst sugarcane growes.
They produce power by burning waste products from the sugarcaine refining process but have been beset by breakdowns and operating problems.
The partnerships said the bankruptcy filing was necessary because of a legal dispute with Florida Power & Light Co over FPL's obligation to buy power produced by the plants.
Lehman said the previous biggest municipal bond defaults in Florida have been "in the $50 to $60 million range, mostly housing-type issues."

Nationally, the defaults would be dwarfed by those linked to New York City's financial difficulties in the mid-1970s, by the $2.25 billion default of Washington Public Power Supply System revenue bonds in 1983 and by Orange County, Calif.'s default two years ago.

Additionally, Lehman said the dollar amount of municipal bond defaults related to financial difficulties at LTV steel and Mutual Benefit Life exceeded the total outstanding on the Palm Beach County, Fla., power plants.
"That (the Florida issues) would be sixth if you counted the Mutual Benefit Life as one default, even though it involved 30 different issues," Lehman said.

It was unclear how the Florida bondholders would be treated by the bankruptcy court under Chapter 11 proceedings. Typically, Lehman said, they would be paid with whatever cash flow remains after operating costs are paid.
The trustee could also decide to sue the plant owners, in which case some of the incoming revenues or escrowed funds could be held back for litigation expenses, Lehman said.
